note: Supports the time (7:30 am), the unit (8th Illinois Cavalry), the officer (Lt. Marcellus Jones) and the place (western yard of the Wisler house, carbine on a fence post) of the first-shot row; the NPS page calls it the first shot of the battle; the row itself notes the claim is symbolic.
The seminary main building was used for weeks after the battle as a hospital for both sides (the row concerns July 1: this passage dates the use only as lasting weeks).
McPherson farmhouse, bank barn, stables and wagon shed sheltered the wounded on July 1 and stayed filled under Confederate control.
A July 5 visitor found the barn, wagon shed, tenant house, pig sty and barnyard crowded with badly wounded men.
The barn sheltered Union regiments, sharpshooters fired from the stone gable walls, and it served as shelter and hospital after the fighting.
The inventory records the barn as a shelter and hospital after the fighting; no burning is mentioned.
The two large Weikert farm buildings were field hospitals during and after the battle for the casualties at Little Round Top and the Wheatfield Road.
Dr. Brinton was in charge of the 2nd Division, 11th Corps hospital at the George Spangler farm where Armistead was taken.
The 1988 study names the 11th Corps hospital at the George Spangler farm as the site of Armistead's death.
The Spangler farm complex served as the 11th Corps field hospital.
The Spangler farm complex served as the 11th Corps field hospital.
Mary Thompson's property, used as Lee's headquarters, lost fencing and had breastworks built and a garden destroyed.
Col. Aiken recalled two fences lining the Emmitsburg Road; the report records worm fencing on the east boundary of the Rose and Snyder fields documented in the 1868 Warren map.
Worm fencing around the Peach Orchard and Rose North Orchard documented in the 1863 Bachelder map, the 1872 survey and photographs.
The study says a post and rail fence paralleled the Emmitsburg Road and that no stone fence is known there (stones may have been piled under the rails).
The park report says the whole west slope of Little Round Top had been cut clear a year before the battle except for a few scattered trees and light undergrowth.
On the Warren map Big Round Top has a heavy growth of round-leaf trees, oak and pine; Brady photographs show the Little Round Top slope nearly bare.
The inventory says the western side of Little Round Top was open at the time of the battle.
